name: Go goroutines vs Intel TBB on a task-graph dynamic program (Comparison-Go-CppTBB)
baseline: Intel oneTBB (2017 Update 3) C++ task scheduler, MSVC v14 build, on the same static optimal binary search tree task graph
workload: Static optimal binary search tree (dynamic programming over a DAG of chunk tasks, problem sizes N=2048 and N=4096, chunking factor VP 1 to 2048, 1 to 8 processors) implemented as goroutines plus channels in Go and as TBB tasks with atomic reference counts in C++.
claimed_speedup: Paper: at N=4096 and 4 processors Go ran faster than TBB at VP=256 and VP=512, with a TBB/Go time ratio of 1.12 and 1.15; best parallel speed-up over each language's own sequential code was 6.28 (Go, N=4096; 6.53 with 4 threads in the conclusion) versus 3.95 (TBB, N=4096; 4.41 with 4 threads). At N=2048 TBB was faster in every condition (paper: 'with fixed N=2048, C++ TBB and Go took 6255.4, 12689.6 ms respectively'; best-case ratio 1.37 in TBB's favour; VP=1: TBB 6488.6 ms, Go 13266.2 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7.4; Intel TBB 2017 Update 3; C++ built with MSVC v14 in Visual Studio 2015 Update 3 (optimisation flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ (4 cores, 8 threads, 6 MB cache), Windows 10 Pro build 14393
tradeoffs: Goroutines come with a garbage-collected runtime and growable stacks; at the highest chunk counts (VP=2048, millions of goroutines) Go lost most of its time in the runtime (up to 84% of CPU time in the worst case, runs from 4.9 s to 66.6 s with 4 processors) while TBB degraded smoothly. Go code is much shorter than the TBB task-graph code.
caveats: Single small experiment: one laptop CPU, Windows, 5 repetitions averaged, 2017 toolchains (Go 1.7.4, TBB 2017U3). The C++ optimisation flags are not stated, so this misses tier A. The paper's own wording is that TBB was faster in general and Go won only partially at the larger size (N=4096, two VP settings, ratio 1.12-1.15). Go's 'superlinear' speed-up (6.3-6.5 on 4 cores) is relative to a Go sequential run that was much slower than the TBB sequential run, so it reflects cache and chunking effects, not a faster scheduler. Venue of the paper (a Korean-language conference paper with an English abstract) is not stated in the PDF, so peer review is not established; the repo is archived and the README says it is no longer updated. Code is under CC-BY-4.0 (not an OSI software licence), so usability is reference. The 2012 Serfass and Tang paper that this repeats is behind a blocked ACM page.
found_via: WebSearch: '"faster than Intel TBB" OR "faster than OpenMP" OR "faster than Taskflow" Rust OR Zig OR Go OR Nim task scheduler thread pool benchmark README' surfaced the repo; opened github.com/luncliff/Comparison-Go-CppTBB (README, tree, commits) and read the checked-in PDF through raw.githubusercontent.com (pdftotext) and docs/Draft.md.
why_faster: Paper's speculation: TBB's atomic reference-counter dependencies and depth-first execution give better locality overall, while Go's channel-based synchronization can trigger many more scheduling events; Go wins only at the larger problem size where its chunked tasks fit the cache better. No single mechanism is claimed for the Go win.

name: Rust std futex-based Mutex (rust-lang/rust PR 95035) vs the pthread_mutex-based std Mutex
baseline: glibc (and musl) pthread_mutex_t, as wrapped by the previous Rust std::sync::Mutex on Linux
workload: matklad/lock-bench: 32 threads, 10,000 lock/unlock operations per thread over 2 (extreme), 64 (heavy), 1,000 (light) or 1,000,000 (no contention) locks, 100 rounds, average time per round.
claimed_speedup: PR comment by m-ou-se on a 64C/128T AMD Threadripper (average per round): extreme contention new 27.65 ms vs old std (gnu pthread) 58.51 ms and old std (musl) 89.15 ms; heavy contention 1.82 ms vs 8.11 ms (gnu) and 7.08 ms (musl); light contention 0.784 ms vs 2.80 ms (gnu) and 2.90 ms (musl); no contention 1.19 ms vs 2.98 ms (gnu) and 2.79 ms (musl). About 2.1x, 4.4x, 3.6x and 2.5x faster than the glibc pthread-based version (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the PR comment; lock-bench is run with cargo run --release (rustc of March 2022, flags otherwise unstated); the glibc and musl pthread builds are distribution builds
stars_or_usage: 119.7k stars (rust-lang/rust); part of the Rust standard library (merged April 2022; the companion RwLock PR 95801 is milestoned 1.62.0)
tradeoffs: A futex-based lock is Linux-specific (the PR targets Linux; other platforms keep their own implementations); one word of state with no heap allocation and a const constructor, but no priority inheritance or robust-mutex support that pthread mutex attributes offer.
caveats: The baseline is the earlier Rust std::sync::Mutex, which called pthread_mutex_t through a heap-allocated box, so part of the gap is Rust-side indirection and the Box allocation rather than glibc's lock algorithm alone; no standalone C program was benchmarked. Single author-posted run on one machine; the comment itself says 'realistic benchmarks are very hard'. In the same table parking_lot::Mutex and spin::Mutex were faster than the new std Mutex under light and no contention (parking_lot 0.695 ms and 0.940 ms, spin 0.605 ms and 0.765 ms), and under extreme contention parking_lot (313 ms) was about 11x slower than the new lock. The tier is C because the numbers sit in a PR comment with no compiler flags; lock-bench itself (matklad/lock-bench) is public and states release mode and a different machine (Intel i7-7820HQ). Only the Mutex has numbers on the PR page; the matching Condvar and RwLock PRs (95801) give none.
found_via: GitHub: pthread-versus-Rust lock idea; opened github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/95035 (title 'Replace Linux Mutex and Condvar with futex based ones.', merged April 2022) and github.com/matklad/lock-bench.
why_faster: PR design: the lock is a single 32-bit futex word (0 unlocked, 1 locked, 2 contended) with a short spin before parking in the kernel and no heap-allocated pthread_mutex_t, so uncontended lock and unlock are one atomic operation each.
